evidence: Draft (nine short sentences): "Decide to do it. How will you coax yourself to do this? Make it spacious? Make it warm and held? etc. Preview what you are going to do. Will you close your eyes? Will you come out and go back in again? What will you do at the end?" Words replaced (SOURCE.txt): "Deciding to do it. How will you coax yourself to do this? Make it spacious? Make it warm and held? Something else? Preview what you are going to do: will you close your eyes? Will you come out and go back in again? What will you do at the end?" Meaning to keep (his published guide): "Decide what kind of encouragement is welcome: spacious listening, warm company, or a firmer invitation to stay with a feeling. Preview eye closure, any repeated exit and re-entry, and the return." PRESERVATION, word by word: the draft differs from the replaced words in exactly three places: 'Deciding' becomes 'Decide'; 'Something else?' becomes 'etc.'; the colon after 'Preview what you are going to do' becomes a full stop (so 'will' is 'Will'). Everything else is word for word the replaced words. The put-back the_change claims, the old 'this' in the second sentence ('How will you coax yourself to do this?'), is there. Nothing is added: no claim, condition, person or number. The three previews (close your eyes; come out and go back in; the end) carry his eye closure, exit and re-entry, and return; 'coax', 'spacious' and 'warm and held' are the replaced words' own rendering of his encouragement and its kinds, untouched by this draft. 'Decide to do it.' is the same step with the same agent (the reader) as the fragment 'Deciding to do it.', now as an imperative; after the safety paragraph's don'ts it reads as the next step, not as pressure, and the stop lines that follow keep the way out. One real difference to tell the author about: his third kind of encouragement, 'a firmer invitation to stay with a feeling', is carried by neither text; the replaced words left a slot for it ('Something else?', a question put to the reader), and 'etc.' is a trailing marker that carries the soft examples on instead of asking about another kind. I count this as within the same meaning, because the opening question 'How will you coax yourself to do this?' still hands the choice to the reader and the change does not claim to put the firmer option back, but it is a small narrowing and the card should not hide it. TELLS, judged in context. T02 is PRESENT: the draft is itself a run of short commands and questions, one job each, handing off to the next, and the paragraph continues in the same cadence with the stop lines. The writer's ABSENT ('one step in its paragraph, not part of a run of compressed commands') does not fit this card, where the draft is the run. I accept it as justified, with an exact reason: this is the before-you-begin planning step, where a run of prompts is the content; the prompts follow his published pair of commands (decide the encouragement; preview eyes, exit and re-entry, return); each is a choice left to the reader, none is a verdict or lesson the text answers; and the replaced paragraph has the identical run, so the change adds no beat and no further compression. Considered and not separately happening: T09/T13 (each question is a different real decision; 'What will you do at the end?' calls back to the earlier 'leaving some time at the end'; 'held' and 'etc.' are the paragraph's own phrasing); T07 ('etc.' marks the options as open in the place the replaced 'Something else?' held, which is a thought, not a stage direction); T12 (spacious and warm-and-held are left open by 'etc.', and the three previews are his own three items, not a symmetry made for balance); T15 (three small edits, none a rarer synonym); T19 ('Preview what you are going to do.' is an instruction to preview as well as the lead-in to its questions, and the replaced words had the same lead-in after a colon); T22 (prompts with steps in them, no reassurance); T25 (the replaced colon is gone). T26: CONTEXT.txt also holds the neighbouring card S24's draft, so four sentences within three paragraphs open with 'Make' ('Make sure you're leaving some time...' in the unchanged text, 'Make sure you're in a safe place...' from card S24, then 'Make it spacious? Make it warm and held?'); S25's own words here are unchanged from the replaced paragraph, so this is not S25's repetition, but the two cards together are worth the author's eye. Other rows (T01, T03-T06, T08, T10, T11, T14, T16-T18, T20, T21, T23, T24, T27-T29, C01-C04) are not happening: no stake, scene, image, aftercare, colon, tic word, closer or invented fact; 'it' and 'this' are the practice the section prepares (C02). LINTER, all six accepted. "B7 short landing at paragraph end": the linter sees the draft alone; in CONTEXT.txt "What will you do at the end?" is followed by the recording line and the stop lines, so it is not a landing. "D9 follows the source order": a rewrite of its own sentences follows their order by construction, and that order is the order of the session's decisions in his published line. "E23 paragraph of instructions": the paragraph prepares the session in steps, as the replaced paragraph and his published one do; the change rewords steps and adds none. "E36/E41 heavy second person" (12.2 'you' per 100): the 'you's are the reader planning their own session, and the replaced words have the same six second-person words. "O29" (run of questions): they are the reader's own previews (his published triad as prompts) and the text does not answer them; the draft adds none and drops one ('Something else?'). "R1" ('Decide to do it.'): 'it' is the practice the section prepares, named in the paragraphs just before ('do this', 'exploratory hypnosis', 'You can do it on something you want to experience more of'); the next sentence says 'this' for the same thing; and the replaced words opened identically ('Deciding to do it.').
